1 Pedro: Curso Intensivo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Born again to a living hope. 1 Peter 1:1–12: the new birth through the resurrection, an inheritance kept in heaven, and trials that prove faith genuine; election "according to the foreknowledge of God" (1:2) with the Calvinist and Arminian readings stated fairly; and how you would preach hope to believers under pressure.

A holy and chosen people. 1 Peter 1:13–2:10: "be holy," redemption by the precious blood of Christ, living stones and a royal priesthood, the priesthood of all believers in your church's life, and the main evangelical views of how the church relates to Israel (2:9–10 drawing on Exodus 19), stated fairly.

Good conduct among unbelievers. 1 Peter 2:11–3:7: citizens, servants, wives and husbands read in their first-century setting; the main evangelical views of 3:1–7 and of roles in marriage (complementarian and egalitarian), stated fairly; and how believers in your setting can live under unjust authority without fear and without compromise.

The suffering Savior and a hard passage. 1 Peter 2:21–25 and 3:18–22: Christ's example and His death for the unrighteous; the main interpretations of His preaching "to the spirits in prison" and of "baptism now saves you," together with the main evangelical views of baptism, stated fairly; and how to preach a difficult passage honestly.

Ready to answer, rejoicing in suffering. 1 Peter 3:13–17 and 4:1–19: giving a reason for the hope within you with gentleness and respect, the "fiery trial," suffering as a Christian and judgment beginning at the house of God, and pastoral care for believers facing hostility where you serve.

Shepherds and the God of all grace. 1 Peter 5: elders who shepherd willingly under the Chief Shepherd, humility, casting every care on God, resisting the devil, and a plan for faithful pastoral leadership in your church, with the main evangelical forms of church government stated fairly.

title.es: Hechos: Curso Intensivo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Pentecost and the work of the Spirit. Acts 2 read with 1:4–8, 8:14–17, 10:44–48 and 19:1–7: the main evangelical understandings of the baptism and filling of the Spirit and of tongues (Pentecostal, charismatic, continuationist, cessationist), stated fairly, and how your church can honor the Spirit and keep its unity.

Preaching like the apostles. The sermons of Acts (for example chapters 2, 3, 13 and 17): what they proclaim about Christ, how they speak differently to Jews and to Gentiles, and a sermon shaped by them for your own setting.

Pattern or report? How to tell what Acts gives as a pattern for every church from what belonged to that moment (for example the shared life of 2:42–47 and 4:32–35, the casting of lots in 1:26), applied to one practice in your church.

Crossing every barrier. Samaria, the Ethiopian, Cornelius and the Jerusalem council (Acts 8, 10–11, 15): how the church crossed ethnic and cultural lines without losing the gospel, and how your church can reach people unlike itself.

Mission and new churches. Paul's journeys (Acts 13–20): his methods, his care for young churches, the appointing of elders (14:23) and his charge to the Ephesian elders (20:17–35), and a plan for mission or church planting from your church.

Suffering and the unstoppable gospel. Opposition, prison and trial (Acts 4–5, 16, 21–28): faithful witness under pressure, God's purpose in hardship, and pastoral care for believers facing hostility where you serve.

title.en: Church Administration and Leadership: Ministry Assignment
title.es: Administración y Liderazgo de la Iglesia: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Servant leadership. Mark 10:35–45, John 13:1–17 and 1 Peter 5:1–4: leading as a steward rather than an owner, the danger of the strongman leader who rules the church as his own (the caudillo), and leadership that serves the flock.

Calling, character and grace. 1 Timothy 3:1–13, Titus 1:5–9 and 2 Timothy 2:1–7, with Plummer: the qualifications of elders and deacons, the leader's own holiness by grace, and the main views on who may serve as pastor, elder or deacon (complementarian, egalitarian and shared-ministry views), stated fairly.
Wisdom for leading. Proverbs 11:14, 15:22 and 27:23, and James 1:5 and 3:13–18: wisdom in speech, in seeking counsel, in planning and in correction, and the leader's private disciplines.
Organizing God's work. Nehemiah 1–6, Exodus 18:13–27 and Acts 6:1–7: prayerful planning, delegation and teams, facing opposition, knowing your limits, and passing the work on to the next generation.

Church order and government. Acts 14:23, 15:1–35 and 20:17–35, and Philippians 1:1: the main forms of church government (episcopal, presbyterian, congregational and others), stated fairly, the roles of pastors, elders, deacons and members, and a simple, clear structure for your church.

Money, records and peace. 2 Corinthians 8:16–24, 1 Corinthians 14:40 and Matthew 18:15–20: honest handling of offerings, with more than one person counting and recording them, the legal registration and records required where you serve, church discipline and peacemaking, and the views on the tithe (a binding command or a guide to generous giving), stated fairly.

title.es: Apologética: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Ready to give an answer. 1 Peter 3:15, Acts 17:16–34 and Jude 3: the purpose and spirit of apologetics; the main methods (classical, evidential, presuppositional, cumulative case) compared fairly; and which approach best serves the people you reach.

Does God exist? Psalm 19 and Romans 1:18–20: the arguments from the existence of the world, its design and the moral law, their strengths and limits, and how you would use them in a real conversation.

Creation, science and Scripture. Genesis 1–2: the young-earth, old-earth and other evangelical views of creation's age and of evolution, compared fairly; what all of them affirm (God the Creator, humanity in His image, the reality of the Fall); and how you would help young people in your church who struggle with these questions.

The resurrection of Jesus. 1 Corinthians 15:1–20 and the Gospel accounts: the historical case, the main alternative explanations and their weaknesses, and how you would present the resurrection in evangelism and at Easter.
Suffering and doubt. Job, Psalm 73 and Romans 8:18–39: the problem of evil, the difference between intellectual answers and pastoral care, and how you would walk with a member who doubts.

Answering the challenges where you serve. The belief systems most common in your community (for example Jehovah's Witnesses, Latter-day Saints, spiritism and folk religion, secular unbelief, or another world religion): a gracious, biblical response, and a plan to equip your church to answer.

title.es: Personajes Bíblicos II: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: John the Baptist, the forerunner. Isaiah 40:3–5, Luke 1 and 3, John 1:19–37 and 3:27–30, and Matthew 11:2–11, with Gibson: the call to repentance, "He must increase, but I must decrease," doubt in prison and Jesus' answer; and the views on how John's baptism relates to Christian baptism (Acts 19:1–7), stated fairly.

Peter, fallen and restored. Matthew 16:13–23, Luke 22:31–62, John 21:15–19, Acts 2 and Galatians 2:11–14, with Bruce: boldness and impulsiveness, denial and restoration, and Peter's later failure at Antioch; and the main readings of "on this rock" (Peter himself, his confession, or Christ), including the Roman Catholic and Protestant views, stated fairly.

Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ. Acts 9, 22 and 26, Philippians 3:4–14 and 2 Corinthians 11:16–12:10, with Stokes: the persecutor turned apostle, suffering and the thorn in the flesh; whether Damascus is better described as a conversion or a call, and the main views of Romans 7 (Paul before or after conversion), stated fairly.

John, the disciple whom Jesus loved. Mark 3:17, Luke 9:51–56, John 13:23, 19:26–27 and 20:24–31, and 1 John 4:7–21, with Dods and Bruce: from "son of thunder" to apostle of love, truth and love held together, Lazarus and Thomas in John's Gospel; and the main views on who wrote the Gospel, the letters and Revelation, stated fairly.

Jonah, the reluctant prophet. Jonah 1–4, Matthew 12:38–41 and Luke 11:29–32: running from God's call, the sign of Jonah, God's mercy to Nineveh and the prophet's anger at it; the main views on how the book is to be read (a straightforward historical account, or history told with features of a parable), stated fairly; and the call to love one's enemies.

Preaching New Testament lives. 1 Corinthians 11:1, Philippians 3:17 and Hebrews 13:7–8: imitating believers as they imitate Christ, the danger of hero worship and of personality cults around leaders, and a sermon series on these lives for your church.

title.es: Personajes Bíblicos: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Preaching a life. Romans 15:4, 1 Corinthians 10:1–13 and Hebrews 11, with Whyte and F. B. Meyer: Bible characters as examples and as witnesses to God's grace, and the debate between preaching them mainly as examples to follow and preaching them mainly as part of the history of redemption that leads to Christ, stated fairly, avoiding both moralism and allegory.

Abraham and the obedience of faith. Genesis 12–22, Romans 4, James 2:21–24 and Hebrews 11:8–19: the call, the covenant, the failures in Egypt and Gerar, and the offering of Isaac; how Paul and James both use Abraham; and the main views of how the promises to Abraham relate to Israel and the church (covenant theology, dispensationalism and positions between them), stated fairly.

Joseph and the hidden hand of God. Genesis 37–50, especially 45:4–8 and 50:20, and Psalm 105:16–22: envy and suffering in a family, temptation, forgiveness and reconciliation; Joseph as a figure of Christ and the limits of typology; and the main views of God's sovereignty and human responsibility, stated fairly.

Moses, the servant of God. Exodus 2–4 and 32–34, Numbers 12:3 and 20:1–13, and Hebrews 3:1–6: formation in the wilderness, intercession, meekness and the failure at Meribah; and the main views of how the law given through Moses applies to Christians, stated fairly.

David, a man after God's heart. 1 Samuel 16–17, 2 Samuel 11–12, Psalm 51 and Acts 13:22: calling, courage and friendship; the sin against Bathsheba and Uriah told honestly, as an abuse of a king's power; repentance and its lasting consequences; and the views on whether and when a fallen leader may return to ministry, stated fairly.

Elijah and the secret of his power. 1 Kings 17–19, James 5:17–18 and Luke 1:17: prayer, courage before Ahab and the prophets of Baal, despair under the broom tree and God's gentle care; caring for exhausted or depressed servants of God, including when to seek medical help; and a sermon series on these lives for your church.

title.en: How We Got the Bible: Ministry Assignment
title.es: Cómo Obtuvimos la Biblia: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Inspiration and authority. What Scripture claims for itself (2 Timothy 3:16–17, 2 Peter 1:19–21) and how Jesus treated the Scriptures (Matthew 5:17–18, John 10:35); the main evangelical ways of stating inerrancy and infallibility, stated fairly; and how you would build your church's confidence in the Bible.

Recognizing the Hebrew Scriptures. How Israel's Scriptures came to be received as one collection (Luke 24:44), why Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Bibles differ on the Apocrypha, stated fairly, and how you would answer a member who asks why some Bibles have more books.

The New Testament canon. The tests the early church used (apostolic origin, agreement with the faith handed down, use across the churches), the church recognizing rather than creating the canon, and how you would answer popular claims about "lost gospels."

Manuscripts and the text. How the text was copied and how scholars compare manuscripts, worked through one passage with a known variant (for example Mark 16:9–20 or John 7:53–8:11), and how to explain it honestly to your congregation without shaking their faith.

Translations and the church. Word-for-word and meaning-for-meaning translation, the Reina-Valera tradition and modern versions in Spanish and English, the debate over the King James and Reina-Valera "only" positions and the underlying Greek text stated fairly, and how you would guide your church in choosing and using translations.

The Bible in the hands of your people. Nehemiah 8, Psalm 119 and Acts 17:11, with the common objections your people hear (contradictions, corruption, "just a human book"), and a plan to help your congregation read, trust and obey Scripture.

title.es: Educación Cristiana: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The teaching ministry of the church. Deuteronomy 6:4–9, Matthew 28:20, Ephesians 4:11–16 and 2 Timothy 2:2: teaching as part of making disciples, the gift and the office of teacher, and the main views on who may teach adults in the church (1 Timothy 2:12), stated fairly.
Jesus the master teacher. Mark 4, Luke 10:25–37 and John 4: Jesus' questions, stories, object lessons and patience with slow learners, with one lesson for your church built on His methods.

How people learn. Proverbs 22:6, Nehemiah 8:7–8 and Luke 2:46–52, with Trumbull's principles: "telling is not teaching," knowing the learner and the lesson, questions and review; children, youth and adults; and teaching people who learn mainly by hearing rather than by reading.

Teaching the faith at home and in the church. Deuteronomy 6, Ephesians 6:4 and 2 Timothy 1:5 and 3:14–15: parents as the first teachers, the use of catechisms from different traditions with discernment, and the views on children's place in the church (when they may be baptized or take the Lord's Supper), stated fairly.

Safe ministry with children and youth. Matthew 18:1–14 and Mark 10:13–16: screening and training of teachers and volunteers, never leaving one adult alone with a child, responding to signs of abuse and reporting it where the law requires, and a written child-protection policy for your church.

Teaching that transforms. Colossians 1:28–29, James 1:22 and Romans 12:2: the aim of Christian education as Christlike life, not information alone, and a curriculum plan for your church (Sunday school, small groups, new believers, leaders) with a way to evaluate it.

title.es: Crecimiento de la Iglesia: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: What true growth is. Acts 2:41–47, Ephesians 4:11–16 and Colossians 1:28: growth in numbers, in maturity and in service, and the main approaches since the 1950s (the Church Growth movement and its "homogeneous unit principle," seeker-sensitive churches, the missional church, church-health models), stated fairly with their critics.

Growth is God's work. 1 Corinthians 3:5–9, Acts 2:47 and John 15:1–8: God gives the growth and uses human means, with the Calvinist and Arminian emphases on God's sovereignty and human response stated fairly, and the place of prayer in your church's plans.

The pattern of Acts. Acts 2:42–47, 6:1–7, 11:19–26 and 13:1–3: what in Acts describes one moment and what sets a pattern for every church, and the cessationist and continuationist views of signs and wonders, stated fairly.

Disciples, not only decisions. Matthew 28:19–20, Mark 3:14 and 2 Timothy 2:2, with A. B. Bruce's The Training of the Twelve: small groups and personal discipleship, and a pathway from new believer to mature disciple and leader in your church.

Healthy churches that reproduce. Acts 14:21–23 and 1 Thessalonians 1:6–8, with Nevius's plan and Allen's principles: churches that lead, support and spread themselves, unpaid local leaders, daughter churches and house or cell churches, and the dangers of dependence.

False growth and real obstacles. 2 Timothy 4:3–4 and Revelation 3:1–6 and 14–22: growth bought with the prosperity message, celebrity, taking members from other churches or chasing numbers; real barriers such as conflict, poor leadership transitions and neglect of the poor; and a growth plan for your congregation.

title.es: Historia de la Iglesia: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Faithful unto death. Polycarp and the early martyrs beside Revelation 2:10 and 1 Peter 4:12–19: what they teach about confessing Christ under pressure, applied to believers in your setting.

Defending the deity of Christ. Nicaea and Athanasius: the question the church faced, the biblical case it made (for example John 1, Colossians 1, Hebrews 1), and how you would answer groups today that deny that Christ is God.

Love for God in the medieval church. Bernard's On Loving God read beside Matthew 22:37–39 and 1 John 4: what is true and useful in it, what should be weighed carefully, and how you would teach love for God in your church.

The Reformation and the gospel. Scripture as the final authority and justification by faith (Romans 3–5, Galatians 2), why the Reformers were willing to suffer, and what their recovery of the gospel means for your church; where Protestants themselves differed, state the views fairly.

Revival and renewal. One awakening or revival (for example the Great Awakening, the Wesleyan revival, or a movement in the history of your own country): what Scripture teaches about renewal, how to weigh such movements, and what your church can learn.
Carey and the church's mission. Carey's call to mission and the Great Commission, the spread of the church to Latin America, Africa and Asia, and your church's part in that mission today.

title.es: Situaciones de Consejería: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Comforting the afflicted. 2 Corinthians 1:3–7, Job and Romans 8:18–39: trusting God's providence without pretending to explain every sorrow, what Job's friends got wrong, the main Christian answers to why God permits suffering, stated fairly, and a plan for visiting the sick and the suffering in your church.

Grief and bereavement. John 11, 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 and 1 Corinthians 15: grieving with hope, the funeral and the months that follow, the mourning customs of your region met with respect and with the gospel, and when grief needs more help than a pastor can give.

The bruised and the fragile. Isaiah 42:3, Matthew 11:28–30 and Psalm 103:13–14: caring for people wounded by abuse, trauma or harsh churches; safety first, the duty to report abuse where the law requires it, and the views on separation and divorce in cases of abuse, stated fairly; and why a victim must never be counseled back into danger.

The downcast. Psalms 42–43, 1 Kings 19 and 2 Corinthians 4:8–18: discouragement, depression and anxiety in body, mind and spirit; the main Christian views on medicine and professional care alongside pastoral counsel, stated fairly; and how to ask about thoughts of suicide and get emergency help, never leaving a person at risk alone.

The tempted and the accused. Ephesians 6:10–18, Romans 8:1 and 31–39, and 1 John 1:9–2:2: recurring temptation, addiction and pornography, accountability that restores rather than shames, assurance with the Calvinist and Arminian views stated fairly, and the main evangelical views of spiritual warfare and deliverance, stated fairly.

Knowing your limits. Exodus 18:13–27, Galatians 6:1–5 and Romans 13:1–4: when and how to refer, confidentiality and its limits, building a list of trusted doctors, counselors and agencies in your community, and caring for your own soul as a counselor.

title.en: Cults and World Religions: Ministry Assignment
title.es: Sectas y Religiones del Mundo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Discernment and the measure of truth. Galatians 1:6–9, 1 John 4:1–3, Acts 17:11 and Jude 3: what makes a teaching "another gospel," the historic creeds as a summary of the faith, and the difference between departures from the gospel and disagreements among Christians (baptism, church government, spiritual gifts, the end times).

Naming groups fairly. 2 Timothy 2:24–26 and 1 Peter 3:15–16: what "cult" means in theology and in sociology, and why the word can wound; and how evangelicals differ in assessing some movements (for example Seventh-day Adventism, Oneness Pentecostalism, Roman Catholicism and the prosperity message), with the main views stated fairly and each group described from its own sources.

Movements that depart on Christ and Scripture. John 1:1–18, Colossians 2:8–10 and Revelation 22:18–19: the Latter-day Saints, Jehovah's Witnesses and the groups active in your own region, described from their own sources, and how added revelation, a different Christ and salvation by works change the gospel.

The great world religions. Acts 17:16–34 and Romans 1:18–2:16: Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism and the folk religion of your region, what each teaches and seeks, true points of contact and real differences, and religious freedom for people of every faith.

The uniqueness of Christ. John 14:6, Acts 4:12 and 1 Timothy 2:5: the incarnation, the cross and the resurrection as what sets the gospel apart, and the main Christian views on those who never hear the gospel (exclusivism, inclusivism and pluralism), stated fairly, including why most evangelicals reject pluralism.

Witness with gentleness and respect. 1 Peter 3:15, Colossians 4:5–6 and 2 Timothy 2:24–26: conversations with neighbors of other faiths and with missionaries at your door, care for people leaving a high-control group, and a plan for teaching your church to discern and to love.

title.en: Deacon Family Ministry Plan: Ministry Assignment

topics.en: The ministry of the deacon. Acts 6:1–7, Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:8–13 and Mark 10:45, with Howell: service before status, the qualifications of deacons and how they are chosen; the deacon's place under the main forms of church government (a governing board, a serving team, and others), stated fairly; and the views on women as deacons or deaconesses (Romans 16:1, 1 Timothy 3:11), stated fairly.

Caring for the needy and vulnerable. Acts 2:44–45, 4:32–35 and 6:1, 1 Timothy 5:3–16, James 1:27 and Matthew 25:31–46, with Edwards's Charity and Its Fruits: widows, orphans, the sick, the elderly and migrants; help that protects dignity; benevolence funds counted and recorded by more than one person; and the views on how the church's care for the poor relates to evangelism, stated fairly.

Knowing and visiting the flock. John 10:1–16, Acts 20:20 and 28, and Ezekiel 34, with Baxter's The Reformed Pastor: sharing the households of the church among the deacons, visits at home and in hospital, listening, keeping confidences and their limits, and knowing when to call the pastor or other help.

Family worship. Deuteronomy 6:4–9, Joshua 24:15, Psalm 78:1–8 and Colossians 3:16, with James W. Alexander and Baxter: Scripture, prayer and song in the home, help for families where reading is hard, for single parents and for homes with one believing spouse, and Brother Lawrence's Catholic classic read with discernment.

Building Christian households. Ephesians 5:21–6:4, Colossians 3:18–21, 1 Peter 3:1–7 and 1 Corinthians 13, with Kingston and Edwards, and Abbott read with discernment: love and example in the home; the complementarian and egalitarian views of marriage, stated fairly; and domestic abuse: safety first, reporting where the law requires it, and referral.

A family ministry plan. Nehemiah 4:14, Psalm 127 and Titus 2:1–8: a written plan for the deacons of your church to care for its families (assigning households, regular visits, help in crisis, resources for family worship, mentoring of young couples and parents), with how it will be reviewed.

title.es: Predicación Doctrinal: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Why preach doctrine? Acts 20:27, 2 Timothy 4:2–4 and Titus 1:9: doctrine as the food of a growing church and its defense against error, the objection that doctrine divides, and a year's plan of doctrinal sermons for your congregation.

From text to doctrine. 2 Timothy 3:16–17 and Acts 17:11: drawing a doctrine from a passage rather than proof-texting, the main evangelical views of the inspiration and authority of Scripture (inerrancy and infallibility), stated fairly, and one doctrine built from several texts in their settings.

Preaching the Trinity and the person of Christ. Matthew 28:19, John 1:1–18 and Philippians 2:5–11: the triune God and the full deity and humanity of Christ, illustrations that distort them, and how you would preach these truths where Oneness and Jehovah's Witness teaching are present.

Preaching the cross and salvation. Isaiah 53, Romans 3:21–26 and Colossians 2:13–15: the main views of the atonement (penal substitution, Christ the Victor, moral influence, and how they relate), justification by faith, and election, with the Calvinist and Arminian views stated fairly, and how you would end a doctrinal sermon with the gospel call.

Preaching where Christians differ. Matthew 28:19, 1 Corinthians 11:23–26 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18: baptism, the Lord's Supper, the gifts of the Spirit or the millennium, with the main views stated fairly, and how to preach a disputed doctrine with conviction and charity, without cowardice and without combat.

Doctrine that leads to worship and life. Romans 11:33–12:2 and Ephesians 1–4: doctrine that ends in praise, doctrine applied to the conscience, and sanctification and assurance with the main evangelical views (Reformed, Wesleyan holiness, Keswick, Pentecostal) compared fairly.

title.en: Baptist History and Denominational Development: Ministry Assignment
title.es: Historia y desarrollo denominacional de los bautistas: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Succession or truth? Matthew 16:18, 1 Kings 19:18 and Romans 11:1–5, with Armitage: what the New Testament means by “church”; the theory of an unbroken visible succession of Baptist churches since the apostles, held by many Baptists (notably in the Landmark tradition), and Armitage's answer that Baptists rest their claim on the New Testament rather than on a chain of churches; the main Baptist accounts of Baptist origins (from the English Separatists, from the Anabaptists, or in a line of dissenting churches), as Baptist historians state them; and teaching this history without inventing or despising it.

Anabaptists, Münster and the sword. Acts 2:38–41, Matthew 5:38–48 and Romans 13:1–7, with Armitage: the case for believer's baptism in the 1520s, the Schleitheim articles (1527), the Peasants' War and the Münster disaster of 1534–1535, Menno Simons's rebuilding, how Baptists have understood their relation to the Anabaptists, and telling the truth about opponents and about one's own side.

John Bunyan and the English Baptists. Acts 4:19–20, 2 Timothy 2:9 and Hebrews 11:13–16, with Armitage: Bunyan's conversion in Grace Abounding, twelve years in Bedford jail for preaching, The Pilgrim's Progress as pastoral theology, and the debate in which Bunyan took part between Baptists who held open communion and those who held closed communion, with both Baptist positions stated fairly.

Roger Williams and soul liberty. Matthew 13:24–30 and 36–43, and John 18:36, with Armitage: Williams on “the field is the world,” the founding of Rhode Island and John Clarke's “lively experiment,” the question of who may baptize, liberty even for those Baptists opposed (the Quakers), and soul liberty in Baptist conviction and practice today.

Baptists and religious liberty in America. Matthew 22:15–22 and Romans 13:1–7, with Armitage: toleration and free exercise, Isaac Backus and John Leland, the Danbury letter and the “wall of separation,” the Baptist record on slavery and the division of 1845 confessed honestly, and voluntary giving and cooperation for mission.

Acts 1:8 and Revelation 7:9–10: how Baptist work came to Mexico, Cuba and the rest of Latin America, the conventions, associations and independent Baptist churches that exist where you serve, how Baptists relate to other evangelicals there, and a lesson series on Baptist history for your church.

title.en: Baptist Theology and Distinctive Doctrines: Ministry Assignment
title.es: Teología bautista y doctrinas distintivas: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Knowing God and His Word. Romans 1:18–2:16, Acts 14:15–17 and 17:22–31, and 2 Timothy 3:14–17, with Dagg: the duty of studying religious truth, the witness of creation and conscience to God, the arguments for His existence after Darwin, the origin and authority of the Bible, and the place of Scripture in the Baptist confessions (the Second London Confession of 1689 and the New Hampshire Confession of 1833).

Creation and the fall. Genesis 1–3, Romans 5:12–21 and Ephesians 2:1–10, with Dagg: creation from nothing, the evangelical views of the days of Genesis 1 that Baptists hold, stated fairly, rest, work and stewardship, humanity's first state, the fall, sin, depravity and condemnation, and the helplessness of the sinner.

The person and states of Christ. Philippians 2:5–11, Hebrews 1–2 and 1 Peter 3:18–22, with Dagg: the humiliation and exaltation of Christ, the debate over what the Son “emptied,” eternal sonship, the main readings of the texts on Christ's descent, stated fairly, and Christ's present work as Priest and King.

God's saving purpose. Ephesians 1:3–14, Romans 8:28–39 and John 6:37–44, with Dagg: the eternal covenant of grace in the purpose of the triune God; election as Calvinistic Baptists such as Dagg teach it and as General and Free Will Baptists teach it, both stated fairly as Baptist views; and why Baptists read the biblical covenants differently from those who baptize infants.

Justification, adoption and perseverance. Romans 3:21–5:1, Galatians 4:4–7 and John 10:27–30, with Dagg: justification by faith alone and the imputation of Christ's righteousness, faith, new birth and works, adoption into God's family, and the Baptist views of perseverance and assurance (the security of the believer, and the Free Will Baptist view that a believer may fall away), stated fairly.

The Holy Spirit and the Baptist distinctives. John 3:1–8, Romans 6:1–4 and 1 Peter 2:4–10, with Dagg: the person and work of the Holy Spirit in new birth and holiness, and how Baptist theology grounds believer's baptism, a regenerate church, the priesthood of all believers and soul liberty; and a plan to teach these doctrines in your church.

title.en: Congregational Church Government and Baptist Polity: Ministry Assignment

topics.en: What a church is. Matthew 16:18 and 18:15–20, Acts 2:41–47 and 1 Corinthians 1:2, with Hiscox: the assembly of God in the Old Testament, the local and the universal church as Baptists understand them, the church covenant, the marks of a true church (the Word, the ordinances and discipline), and liberty of conscience as a Baptist witness and a pastor's duty.

A regenerate membership. Acts 2:37–47, Romans 6:1–4, Romans 14:1–15:7 and 1 Peter 2:4–10, with Hiscox: membership by profession of faith and baptism, receiving and dismissing members and letters of commendation, children and households as Baptists read the hard cases, the Baptist views of who may come to the Lord's Table (closed, close and open communion), stated fairly, and making membership meaningful again.

Pastors and deacons. Acts 6:1–7 and 20:17–38, 1 Timothy 3:1–13, Titus 1:5–9 and 1 Peter 5:1–4, with Hiscox: the two offices Baptists recognize and their qualifications, ordination in Baptist life, and the views held among Baptists on a single pastor or a plurality of elders and on women as deacons and as pastors, stated fairly; and the care of the pastor.

Congregational government. Acts 1:15–26, 6:1–6 and 15:1–35, and 2 Corinthians 2:6, with Hiscox: why Baptists hold that each congregation governs itself under Christ, church independence, associations and conventions for cooperation, what to do when independence goes wrong, and the church business meeting as an act of worship.

Church discipline in love. Matthew 18:15–20, 1 Corinthians 5, 2 Corinthians 2:5–11 and Galatians 6:1, with Hiscox: private and public offenses, a case followed from start to finish, discipline in the Baptist record books, restoration as the goal, and sin that is also a crime: abuse must always be reported to the authorities.

Church order where you serve. Titus 1:5 and 1 Corinthians 14:40: a church constitution and covenant, the legal registration required where you serve (for example as an asociación religiosa in Mexico), membership classes, and a written plan to strengthen membership, leadership and discipline in your church.

topics.en: The text is a trust. Nehemiah 8:8, 2 Corinthians 4:2 and 2 Timothy 2:15, with Broadus: choosing and interpreting a text, his rules tested on three well-loved verses, types and allegory and the line Broadus drew, disputed passages (such as Mark 16:9–20 and John 7:53–8:11) handled honestly in the pulpit, the open Bible and the Baptist conscience, and a week from study to pulpit.

Luke 24:27 and 32, Acts 8:30–35 and Matthew 13:34–35, with Broadus: explaining a passage and a doctrine (justification by faith) plainly, honest silence where Scripture is silent, pictures in the prophets before the parables, and Baptist masters of the homely illustration such as Bunyan and Spurgeon.

Acts 2:14–41 and 16:25–34, with Broadus: where the sermon outline came from, one passage arranged three ways, proportion, arranging for listeners who hear rather than read, and the public invitation in Baptist history, with the views held among Baptists on how to close a sermon stated fairly.

Free-church worship. John 4:23–24, 1 Corinthians 14:26–40 and 1 Timothy 4:13, with Broadus: prepared thought and free words, ordering a free-church service with freedom and form, the public reading of Scripture, learning public prayer from the prayers of the Bible, and congregational song.

topics.en: The commission still binding. Matthew 28:18–20, Luke 24:46–49 and Acts 1:8, with Carey: the commission read closely, one mission from Genesis to Revelation, the hyper-Calvinist objection and Andrew Fuller's answer to “the modern question,” whether the apostles finished the task, and why Calvinistic and Arminian Baptists alike hold the commission binding on every church.

The gospel on the move. Acts 11:19–26, 13:1–3 and 14:21–28, with Carey: Antioch as the first sending church, Paul's way of planting churches and entrusting them to local leaders, the history Carey could not see, Black Baptists who went before him (among them George Liele in Jamaica), and Asian, African, Caribbean and Latin American believers who became missionaries.

A map of the world. Genesis 10, Psalm 67 and Revelation 7:9–10, with Carey's survey of 1792: the nations in Scripture, peoples as well as countries, the shift of the church's center to the Majority World, Baptists of the Majority World, the Bible in every language, and the gospel and culture (dignity, contextualization and the danger of mixing the gospel with other beliefs).

The called minister and the cost. Exodus 3–4, 1 Corinthians 9 and 2 Corinthians 11:23–29, with Carey: objections answered, the Baptist theology of the called minister, suffering in mission, the cost to families (Dorothy Carey) and the care of missionary families, the Serampore Form of Agreement (1805), and self-supporting ministry in the Majority World.

Pray, organize, give. Matthew 9:35–38, 2 Corinthians 8–9 and Philippians 4:10–20, with Carey: the call to prayer of 1784 behind the meeting at Kettering, “expect great things; attempt great things,” the society or the church as the sending body and the Baptist debates over it, cooperative giving, integrity and accountability, and the “rope-holders” who sustain those who are sent.

title.es: Historia y desarrollo del pentecostalismo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The Pentecostal baptism restored. Joel 2:23–29, Acts 2 and 19:1–7, with The Apostolic Faith: restoration as the first Pentecostals told church history, how Charles Parham's Bible school in Topeka reached its teaching of tongues as the “Bible evidence” (1901), the classical Pentecostal teaching of initial evidence and of the baptism in the Spirit as an experience after conversion, faith homes and living by faith, and telling the truth about a founder, Parham included.

Azusa Street. Acts 2:1–21 and 10:34–35, and James 2:1–9, with The Apostolic Faith: the meetings at 312 Azusa Street from 1906 under William J. Seymour, revival without human machinery, “no respect of persons” at the altar across lines of race, the African American roots of Azusa worship, the testimony meeting, singing in the Spirit and with the understanding, and children in a Pentecostal church.

Origins, leadership and belief. Acts 12:12, Acts 17:26 and Matthew 25:46, with The Apostolic Faith: the cottage prayer meeting on Bonnie Brae Street, Seymour preaching what he was still seeking, women in the first Pentecostal ministry, Christ as head of the church, “one blood” against theological racism, and the mission's teaching on eternal punishment.

The three blessings and the spreading fire. Leviticus 25, Luke 4:16–21 and 24:49, and Matthew 13:31–32, with The Apostolic Faith: the year of jubilee, Azusa's “pardon, purity and power” and the later Finished Work debate among Pentecostals, tarrying for the Spirit, faith and medicine, and the practices that kept the unity of the Spirit.

A movement goes global. Acts 8, 11:19–26 and 13:1–3, with The Apostolic Faith: how the paper itself spread the movement, the letters that built it, G. B. Cashwell, C. H. Mason, A. J. Tomlinson and William Durham carrying it into the churches that became the Pentecostal Holiness Church, the Church of God in Christ and the Church of God, and later the Assemblies of God (1914); testing leaders in a fast-growing movement; and faith missions and the care of those who are sent.

topics.en: Testimony and theology. Acts 2:1–4, 22:1–21 and 26:1–23, and Luke 24:49, with Durham: his conversion, his baptism in the Spirit at Azusa Street in 1907 and his call; the holiness world that formed him; Parham, Seymour and the doctrine of initial evidence; testimony as a source of Pentecostal theology, tested by Scripture; and tarrying for the Spirit.

Two experiences, not two works. Acts 2, 8:14–17, 9:17–18, 10:44–48 and 19:1–7, and 1 Corinthians 12:13, with Durham: what is at stake in the baptism in the Spirit as an experience after conversion, five scenes in Acts read closely, Paul's language of sealing, baptism and indwelling, water baptism in Durham's order, the three-stage case of the Wesleyan Pentecostals at its strongest, and other evangelical and charismatic readings, stated fairly.

The Finished Work. Romans 6, Hebrews 10:10–14 and 1 Corinthians 1:30, with Durham: how Scripture speaks of sanctification, Wesley's doctrine stated fairly, Durham's teaching that the believer is sanctified in Christ at conversion and grows in holiness, other evangelical maps of sanctification, and the two Pentecostal families that divided over it: Wesleyan Pentecostal churches (such as the Church of God and the Pentecostal Holiness Church) and Finished Work churches (such as the Assemblies of God).

Answering critics. John 17:17–19, and 1 Corinthians 1–3 and 13, with Durham: naming experience, Durham's rule of “chapter and verse,” consecration and cleansing in the word “sanctify,” carnal and spiritual believers, and leaders, loyalty and factions; and, after Durham, the Oneness controversy of 1913–1916 and the Trinitarian answer of the Assemblies of God's Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916).

The Azusa Street dispute of 1911. Matthew 18:15–17, Acts 15 and 3 John 9–10, with Durham and Seymour: reading a church quarrel as history, Seymour as pastor and theologian, authority in the local church, the place of race in the breakdown of Azusa's unity, judging claims about another's heart, and what both Pentecostal families inherited.

title.es: El Espíritu Santo, los dones espirituales y el discernimiento: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The promise of the Father. Luke 24:49, Acts 1:4–8 and 2:38–39, with Seymour: Seymour as pastor, the promise of the Father in Luke and Acts, seeking the promise rather than the sign, Seymour's order of salvation, sanctification and the baptism in the Spirit and the wider Pentecostal discussion of it, tongues as sign, evidence or gift, missionary tongues and the humility of learning languages, and clean vessels.

Gifts in the body of Christ. 1 Corinthians 12–14, Romans 12:3–8 and Ephesians 4:7–16, with The Apostolic Faith: Paul's Corinth, the gift lists compared, one Spirit and one body (1 Corinthians 12:13), the continuation of the gifts as Pentecostals hold it, with the cessationist reading of “when that which is perfect is come” answered fairly, the “full gospel” and Mark 16:9–20 in context, and order without quenching the Spirit.

Prophecy, tongues and interpretation. 1 Corinthians 14, 1 Thessalonians 5:19–21 and Acts 21:9–14, with The Apostolic Faith: prophecy across the Bible, how authoritative New Testament prophecy is and why it is weighed by Scripture, what the interpretation of tongues is, praying “with the understanding also,” lessons from church history, and a pastoral practice of weighing prophecy in your church.

John 17:17, 1 Corinthians 13 and 1 Timothy 6:3–10, with The Apostolic Faith: Word and Spirit together, sanctification as crisis and process, love as the measure of holiness, gifts without life, money and ministry handled openly and accountably, and testing a call.

topics.en: The call to preach. Isaiah 41:14–16, Jeremiah 1:4–10 and Acts 13:1–3, with Woodworth-Etter: reading testimony as a kind of writing, her call amid grief and suffering, a clean heart and power in her holiness roots, testing a call by inward conviction and outward confirmation, and study, notes and the Spirit together in preparation.

Revival campaigns. 2 Chronicles 7:14, Ezra 9–10 and Acts 2:41–47, with Woodworth-Etter: the revival tradition she inherited, revival in Scripture, calling the church to repentance first, teams and partnership and their breakdown, disaster, providence and prayer, and bringing converts into baptism, membership and church order.

The altar and the manifestations. 1 Kings 18:36–39, Acts 10:9–16 and 2 Corinthians 3:6, with Woodworth-Etter: the mourners' bench and the anxious-bench debate (Finney and Nevin), falling, trembling and weeping in revival history, trances in Scripture, judgment and urgency without manipulation, and testimony, order and care in the gathered church.

Divine healing and discernment. Isaiah 53:4–5, Matthew 8:16–17 and James 5:13–16, with Woodworth-Etter: the divine healing movement before Pentecost, healing in the atonement as Pentecostals teach it, prayer, oil and medicine together, testing signs, wonders and predictions, and pastoral care when healing does not come.

Your daughters shall prophesy. topics.en: Tongues and the nations. Acts 2:1–13, 1 Corinthians 14:1–25 and Revelation 7:9–10: the Pentecostal teaching that the Spirit came at Pentecost to empower witness to every people; the early Azusa hope of "missionary tongues" and why Pentecostal missionaries turned to the patient work of learning languages; and the Pentecostal and other evangelical readings of tongues, stated fairly.

The Holy Spirit as overseer. Acts 13:1–4, 15:28 and 20:28, Ephesians 4:11–13 and 1 Timothy 3:1–13: the Pentecostal conviction that the Spirit calls and anoints leaders, how that conviction relates to offices, credentials and the forms of church government Pentecostal bodies have mixed (episcopal, presbyterian and congregational), and the danger of the founder, "apostle" or prophet who answers to no one.

Accountability that works. 1 Timothy 5:17–22, 2 Corinthians 8:16–24 and Galatians 6:1–2: offerings counted and recorded by more than one person, discipline and the restoration of fallen ministers, the callings of women in Pentecostal history and the views on women in pastoral leadership, stated fairly, and planning for succession.

Trusting God for the work. Matthew 10:9–10, Acts 18:1–4, 1 Corinthians 9:1–18 and Philippians 4:10–19: the Azusa "faith line," tentmaking, the indigenous-church principles of self-support, self-government and self-propagation, the difference between trusting God for provision and the prosperity message, and sending missionaries from Latin America and Africa.

Every mission its own elders. Acts 14:21–23 and 15:1–35, and Titus 1:5: appointing local leaders; unity and freedom among independent missions; the first Pentecostal controversies (the "finished work" and Oneness questions) as tests of how doctrine and fellowship are kept; and Pentecostal church-planting movements in Latin America and Africa.

Honest reports. Luke 1:1–4, Acts 2:41 and 4:4, 2 Samuel 24 and Ephesians 4:25: truthfulness as part of holiness, testing claims of healing with faith and love, counting the global movement honestly, and a plan for truthful reporting in your church or mission.

title.en: History of the Reformation and Reformed Churches: Ministry Assignment

topics.en: Knowing God and knowing ourselves. Romans 1:18–32, Psalm 19 and Acts 17:22–31, with Institutes I.1–5: the shape of the Institutes as a whole, the "sense of divinity" and the Reformed debate over natural theology, and the Reformed teaching that God is to be worshipped only as He has commanded (the regulative principle).

Scripture and the witness of the Spirit. 2 Timothy 3:14–17, 2 Peter 1:19–21 and 1 Corinthians 2:6–16: Calvin's "spectacles," God's accommodation in speaking to us, the Reformed teaching on the inner witness of the Spirit, the canon and the place of evidence, and how Reformed churches have answered claims of new prophecy, with continuationist views stated fairly.

The triune God and His providence. Genesis 50:20, Matthew 10:29–31, Romans 8:28 and Isaiah 45:7: the Trinity as Calvin confessed it with Nicaea, the image of God, the Reformed doctrine of providence and the problem of evil, with other evangelical views stated fairly, and providence as comfort in suffering.

Ruin and remedy. Romans 5:12–21, Ephesians 2:1–10 and John 6:44: original sin, the corruption of the whole person and the bound will as the Reformed churches teach them; the Synod of Dort (1618–1619) and its answer to the Remonstrants, with the Arminian view stated fairly; and common grace.

Justification by faith alone. Romans 3:21–4:8, Philippians 3:7–11 and James 2:14–26: Calvin's "main hinge of religion," imputed righteousness, union with Christ and the "double grace" of justification and sanctification; the Council of Trent's answer and today's debates (including the New Perspective on Paul), stated fairly; and rest for troubled consciences.

From Geneva to Latin America. Calvin's Geneva and its Academy, the Reformed churches of France, the Netherlands and Scotland, the Puritans and the Westminster Assembly, and Presbyterian and Reformed missions in Mexico and Latin America: what this history teaches Reformed churches about persecution, unity and division, and how you would teach it to your church.

topics.en: Union with Christ by the Spirit. John 15:1–11, Romans 6:1–11 and Ephesians 1:13–14: the Reformed teaching that all Christ's benefits come to us as the Spirit unites us to Him; faith and assurance, a debate inside the Reformed family from Calvin to Westminster; and repentance and the two kinds of sorrow (2 Corinthians 7:10).

Not our own. Romans 12:1–2, Titus 2:11–14, Hebrews 12:1–11 and Matthew 16:24: Calvin's teaching on the Christian life (freedom before holiness, self-denial, bearing the cross, meditation on the life to come and the right use of the present life and its callings), and confession and the keys in Reformed practice.

Fruit, not root. Ephesians 2:8–10, Titus 3:4–8, Galatians 3:1–5 and James 2:14–26: good works, merit and rewards; how God crowns His own gifts; the long debate with Rome and within Protestantism; and legalism and its opposite, the neglect of God's law, in the church today.

Unconditional election. Romans 9, Ephesians 1:3–14, John 6:37–44 and Acts 13:48: election as the Reformed churches confess it, the debates inside the Reformed family over the order of God's decrees, the Arminian, Lutheran and other evangelical answers, stated fairly, and preaching election without fear or pride.

Called and kept. John 6:44 and 10:27–29, Romans 8:28–39, Philippians 1:6, and Hebrews 6:4–8 and 10:26–39: effectual calling, the three grounds of assurance, the perseverance of the saints, the warning passages, and other evangelical answers on perseverance, stated fairly.

The hope of glory and the doctrines of grace in the church. 1 Corinthians 15, Romans 8:18–25 and Philippians 3:20–21: the resurrection body and the last things; the "five points of Calvinism" (often summarized as TULIP) and their limits as a summary of Reformed teaching; and a teaching plan on the doctrines of grace that leads your church to humility, assurance and mission.

topics.en: Scripture and the subordinate standard. Confession chapter 1, 2 Timothy 3:16–17, 2 Peter 1:19–21 and Isaiah 8:20: how Presbyterians hold the Confession as a standard under Scripture, what confessional subscription means, and inspiration, preservation and interpretation in later Reformed thought.

God and His eternal decree. Confession chapters 2–5, Ephesians 1:11, Acts 2:23 and 4:27–28, and Romans 9: God's attributes, the Trinity, the decree, creation and providence; how the Confession speaks of God's decree without making Him the author of sin; and other evangelical views, stated fairly.

One covenant of grace. Confession chapters 6–8, Genesis 3:15 and 17:1–14, Jeremiah 31:31–34, Romans 5:12–21, Galatians 3 and Hebrews 8: the covenant of works and the one covenant of grace under different administrations; Christ the Mediator; the Reformed teaching on the extent of the atonement (particular redemption); and other views, including dispensationalism and New Covenant theology, stated fairly.

Grace that grows and keeps. Confession chapters 13–18, Romans 6–8 and 2 Peter 1:3–11: sanctification, Romans 7 and the believer's war, faith and repentance, good works, perseverance and assurance; the Marrow controversy in Scotland; and the care of anxious souls.

Lord of the conscience. Confession chapters 19–24, Exodus 20, Deuteronomy 12:32, Romans 14 and Colossians 2:16–23: the threefold division of the law, Christian liberty ("God alone is Lord of the conscience"), the regulative principle of worship, the Lord's Day, marriage, and church and state from Scotland to Mexico.

Signs, seals and the last day. Confession chapters 25–33, Matthew 18:15–20 and 28:19, 1 Corinthians 11:17–34 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18: the sacraments as signs and seals; infant baptism, with the Baptist reply stated fairly; the Lord's Supper among the main views; discipline and church government; the intermediate state, the resurrection and the judgment; and a plan to teach the Shorter Catechism in your church.

topics.en: Christ the Head and the officers He gives. Isaiah 9:6–7, Ephesians 1:20–23 and 4:7–16, and Colossians 1:18: Christ's kingship over His church and the "two kingdoms"; the officers named in the Form of Government (pastors, teachers, ruling elders and deacons) and its teaching that apostles and prophets have ceased; and the questions Presbyterians still debate about ruling elders and deacons.

Many congregations, one government. Acts 15, Matthew 16:19 and 18:15–20, 1 Corinthians 5 and 2 Corinthians 2:5–11: session, presbytery and synod; the keys of the kingdom; discipline that restores; appeals and the limits of church power; the Presbyterians and Independents at Westminster; and other forms of church government, stated fairly.

Set apart by the laying on of hands. Acts 6:1–6 and 13:1–3, 1 Timothy 4:14 and 5:22, and 2 Timothy 2:2: the inward and outward call, examination, what ordination is and is not, vows and confessional subscription, the people's call and consent, and ordination in mission and emergency.

Reading, prayer and preaching. Nehemiah 8:1–8, Acts 2:42, 1 Timothy 4:13 and Colossians 3:16: the Directory's order for public reading, prayer and preaching; the regulative principle in worship today; the singing of psalms and the debate over hymns, stated fairly; and the Lord's Day, marriage and burial in the Directory.

A seal of the covenant of grace. Genesis 17, Acts 2:38–39, Colossians 2:11–12 and 1 Corinthians 7:14: baptism as the Reformed churches understand it, the covenant case for baptizing the children of believers and household baptisms, the Baptist reply stated fairly, and living out baptism and charity across the divide.

topics.en: Take heed to yourselves. Acts 20:28, 1 Timothy 4:16 and 2 Corinthians 13:5, with Baxter: the pastor's own soul; unconverted ministers in Scripture and history; self-examination and assurance in Reformed teaching; the Puritan means of grace for pastors; and piety and learning joined.

Preaching for use. 2 Timothy 4:1–5, Nehemiah 8:8 and 1 Corinthians 2:1–5: the plain style of William Perkins and the Westminster Directory, doctrine and its "uses," preaching to one person in private conversation, and preaching where you serve.

Pastors who confess first. Ezra 9, Daniel 9:3–19, James 3:1 and 1 Peter 5:1–4: Baxter's confession of the pastors' sins (pride, negligence, love of money and of power); church discipline as the neglected mark of the church; the test of 1662; and humiliation that leads to renewal.

Acts 20:17–38, Romans 10:14–17 and Matthew 28:18–20: Baxter's answers to the objections and today's excuses, his faithfulness after the Great Ejection of 1662, the Reformed missionary tradition from John Eliot to the Presbyterian and Reformed churches of Latin America, and a plan for visitation, catechizing and outreach where you serve.

topics.en: Holy living and the fear of death. Hebrews 2:14–15 and 1 Corinthians 15:55–57, with the Journal: Epworth, Susanna Wesley and the holy-living writers, the Holy Club, the voyage to Georgia and the Moravians who were "not afraid to die"; Wesley's early theology and how he later read his own story.

A parish in the wilderness. Acts 17:26–27, Galatians 3:28 and 1 Timothy 3:1–7: Wesley's plan to restore the primitive church in Georgia, the small societies and hymns that he later called the second rise of Methodism, the gospel among the peoples of Georgia, Wesley's long road to his Thoughts upon Slavery (1774), and the Sophy Hopkey affair as a case in pastoral ethics.

A heart strangely warmed. Romans 1:16–17, 5:1 and 8:15–16, with Luther's preface to Romans: Peter Böhler, Aldersgate (May 24, 1738) and what changed (justification, the new birth and assurance); the instantaneous and the gradual in Wesleyan teaching; and how Methodists and others have read Aldersgate, stated fairly.

Field preaching and free grace. Luke 4:18–19 and 1 Corinthians 9:19–23: Bristol in 1739 and the turn to preaching in the fields; Wesley's sermon "Free Grace" and the break with Whitefield, with the Calvinist view stated fairly; testing revival phenomena; and "the world is my parish" and church order.

Acts 1:8 and 2 Timothy 2:2: the Christmas Conference of 1784 and Methodism in America, the holiness movement and the Church of the Nazarene (1908), Wesleyan and Free Methodist churches, Methodism in Mexico and Latin America, and what this history asks of your church.

topics.en: Grace the source, faith the condition. Ephesians 2:8–10 and Acts 26:28, with "Salvation by Faith" and "The Almost Christian": the Wesleyan teaching on prevenient grace traced through Scripture, grace and freedom in the church's long debate (Augustinian, Reformed and Arminian views, stated fairly), a present salvation, and ministry to nominal faith.

Awake, thou that sleepest. Ephesians 5:14 and Acts 4:31, with Charles Wesley's sermon and "Scriptural Christianity": the spiritual senses, Charles Wesley's hymns as sung theology, the church in Acts as a pattern, the optimism of grace, and prophetic preaching to the church.

God justifies the ungodly. Romans 4:1–8 and 10:5–10, with "Justification by Faith" and "The Righteousness of Faith": justification as pardon, the Church of England's Articles and Homilies, the debate over imputed righteousness, final justification and the controversy over the Minutes of 1770, and preaching justification to the ungodly today.

Righteousness, peace and joy. Mark 1:15, Romans 8:1–17 and 14:17, and Galatians 5:16–25, with "The Way to the Kingdom" and "The First-Fruits of the Spirit": heart religion between formalism and enthusiasm, repentance before and after faith, flesh and Spirit, sin in believers, and the hope of entire sanctification.

Romans 8:14–17 and Galatians 4:4–7, with "The Spirit of Bondage and of Adoption" and "The Witness of the Spirit": how Wesley's teaching on assurance developed, Romans 7 and the three states, assurance in other traditions, stated fairly, testing spiritual experience, and shepherding the doubting and the overconfident.

The way of salvation. Ephesians 2:1–10, Titus 3:4–7 and 1 Thessalonians 5:23–24: prevenient, justifying and sanctifying grace as one way of salvation in Wesleyan teaching, the place of Scripture, reason, tradition and experience in Wesley's method, and a teaching plan on the way of salvation for your church.

topics.en: One design, one desire. Genesis 17:1, Deuteronomy 6:5 and 30:6, and Matthew 5:48 and 6:22: the biblical words behind "perfection" (tamim and teleios), purity of intention, Wesley's teachers (Taylor, à Kempis and Law), his sermon "The Circumcision of the Heart" (1733), the change of 1738 from striving to receiving, and how other traditions hear the call to whole devotion.

Sung and settled. Ezekiel 36:25–29, Colossians 3:16 and Psalm 51:10: Charles Wesley's hymns of perfect love, the early Methodist Conferences on sanctification, and the instantaneous and the gradual in the work of sanctification.

Pure love reigning alone. 1 John 1:7–9 and 3:8–9, and Romans 12:1–2: Wesley's Thoughts on Christian Perfection (1759), the London revival and its excesses, testimony to entire sanctification and its dangers, and how Wesley corrected enthusiasm without giving up the doctrine.

Wesley's mature summary and its heirs. 1 Thessalonians 5:23–24, Philippians 3:12–15 and Hebrews 6:1: Wesley's final summary, growth in love after entire sanctification, the later holiness movement (Phoebe Palmer and the Church of the Nazarene) and where it differed from Wesley, and the Reformed, Keswick and Pentecostal views of sanctification, stated fairly.

Watching over one another in love. Galatians 6:1–2, Hebrews 10:24–25 and James 5:16: the General Rules (do no harm, do good, attend upon the ordinances of God), class meetings, membership vows and loving discipline today.

topics.en: The heart of the evangelist. Romans 9:1–3 and 10:1, 2 Corinthians 5:11–21 and Acts 20:31, with Bonar and Spurgeon: compassion for the lost, prayer, the preacher's own walk with Christ, and the difference between love for souls and love for numbers.

The message we proclaim. 1 Corinthians 2:1–5 and 15:1–8, and Acts 2:14–41 and 17:22–31, with Taylor and Whitefield: sin, the cross, the resurrection, repentance and faith; the main views of the atonement and how each shapes gospel preaching, stated fairly; and adding nothing to the gospel, whether works or the promise of wealth and health.

The freeness of the invitation. John 6:37, Matthew 11:28–30, Isaiah 55:1–7 and Revelation 22:17, with Bunyan: the sincere offer of Christ to all; the Calvinist and Arminian views of election, grace and the free offer, stated fairly; and how preachers in both traditions call sinners freely to Christ.

Acts 2:37–41, 2 Corinthians 5:20 and Joshua 24:15, with Baxter and Alleine: urgency without manipulation; the views on the public invitation or altar call and on other ways of calling for a response (inquiry rooms, personal conversation, baptism), stated fairly; and the care of those who respond.

Preaching in the power of God. 1 Thessalonians 1:5, 1 Corinthians 2:4 and Acts 1:8 and 4:29–31, with Wesley's Journal and Torrey: dependence on the Spirit, prayer and fasting, and revival; the views on a baptism or filling of the Spirit for service, stated fairly; and the difference between the Spirit's power and emotional pressure.

Evangelistic preaching where you serve. Acts 14:8–18 and 17:16–34, and 1 Corinthians 9:19–23: preaching to nominal Christians, to people shaped by popular religion and to the secular; open-air, funeral and campaign settings; judging results honestly; and a plan for an evangelistic sermon series with follow-up and discipleship in your church.

title.es: Gálatas: Curso Intensivo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: No other gospel. Galatians 1:1–2:14: Paul's apostolic calling, the curse on "a different gospel" (1:6–9) and the confrontation at Antioch, and how you would recognize and answer "another gospel" in your setting (for example legalism or the prosperity message) with both firmness and grace.

Justified by faith, not by works of the law. Galatians 2:15–21: what Paul means by "works of the law" and "justified," the traditional Reformation reading and the "New Perspective on Paul" stated fairly, the debate over "faith in Christ" or "the faithfulness of Christ" (2:16), and how you would preach these verses clearly.

The promise and the purpose of the law. Galatians 3: Abraham's faith, Christ who became a curse for us (3:13), why the law was given (3:19–25), and the main evangelical views of how the law applies to Christians (covenant theology, dispensationalism, new covenant theology), stated fairly, with what 3:28 means for unity across ethnic and social lines in your church.

Sons and heirs, not slaves. Galatians 4: adoption and the Spirit who cries "Abba, Father," Paul's use of Hagar and Sarah (4:21–31) and how it differs from allegory of the kind that reads anything into a text, and how you would counsel believers drawn back to rules, rituals or special days (4:9–11).

Freedom, the flesh and the Spirit. Galatians 5: liberty that is not license, the warning of "fallen from grace" (5:4) with the Calvinist and Arminian readings on perseverance stated fairly, the struggle of flesh and Spirit (5:16–17) with the main evangelical views of sanctification compared fairly, and the fruit of the Spirit in your congregation's life together.

Bearing burdens and glorying in the cross. Galatians 6: restoring the fallen gently (6:1–5), supporting those who teach (6:6), sowing and reaping without turning it into a promise of wealth, the new creation, and the main readings of "the Israel of God" (6:16), stated fairly.

title.es: Génesis: Curso Intensivo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Creation, the image of God and human vocation. Genesis 1–2, Psalm 8 and Colossians 1:15–20, with Dods: Genesis 1 as a confession of faith among the creation stories of the nations, the garden as God's sanctuary, and the main readings of the image of God; the young-earth, old-earth, framework and other evangelical views of the days of creation, stated fairly; and the dignity of work, rest and stewardship.

Sin, judgment and grace. Genesis 3–11, Romans 5:12–21 and 2 Peter 2:4–9: the first promise of a Redeemer (3:15) traced through the Bible, Cain and Lamech, and the main views of “the sons of God” (6:1–4) and of the extent of the flood, stated fairly; the curse on Canaan (9:20–27), once misused to defend slavery and racism, read as the text actually says; and the Table of Nations as one humanity in many peoples.

Abraham, the father of faith. Genesis 12–22, Romans 4, Galatians 3:6–9 and Hebrews 11:8–19, with Dods: the missionary heart of the promise (12:1–3), Melchizedek, Abraham the intercessor (18:22–33), his repeated failures and God's protection of the promise, the offering of Isaac, and how Paul, James and Hebrews each use Abraham.

Isaac and Jacob: grace for the undeserving. Genesis 24–35, Hosea 12:2–6, John 1:51 and Romans 9:10–13, with Dods: second-generation faith, prayer and guidance in Genesis 24, favoritism and deceit in a divided family, Bethel and Peniel; and the main views of what Romans 9 draws from Jacob and Esau (the election of individuals to salvation, or the calling of peoples to a role in God's plan), stated fairly.

Joseph: providence and forgiveness. Genesis 37–50, especially 45:4–8 and 50:20, and Acts 7:9–16, with Dods: the art of the story, Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38), faithfulness in a foreign land, the hard question of Joseph's famine policy (47:13–26), forgiveness that tests before it trusts, and how far Joseph may be read as a pattern of Christ.

Preaching Genesis today. Genesis with Hebrews 11 and Luke 24:27: Mosaic authorship and the main critical theories of how Genesis was composed, stated fairly; reading Genesis beside the texts of the ancient Near East; preaching its narratives without moralizing or allegorizing them; and a sermon series through Genesis for your church.

title.es: Hermenéutica: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The heart of the interpreter. Psalm 119:18, John 7:17 and 1 Corinthians 2:10–16: the Spirit's illumination, humility and a readiness to obey as part of interpretation, and a plan to teach your church to read Scripture prayerfully and carefully.

Context and the plain sense. One often-misused verse (for example Jeremiah 29:11, Philippians 4:13 or Matthew 18:20) read in its context: how the misreading arises, what the verse means, and how you would correct the misreading gently in your church.

Reading each book by its kind. Narrative, law, poetry, prophecy, parable, letter and apocalyptic writing: how each is read, with one passage of a kind you seldom preach worked through from observation to application.

Israel's Scriptures in the New Testament. How the apostles use earlier Scripture (for example Matthew 2:15, Acts 2, Hebrews 8), typology as distinct from allegory, and the main evangelical ways of relating the covenants (covenant theology, dispensationalism and positions between them), stated fairly.

Prophecy and the last things. Interpreting prophetic and apocalyptic passages (for example Daniel 9, Matthew 24, Revelation 20): literal and symbolic readings and the main millennial views stated fairly, and how to preach these passages without speculation.

From meaning to application. Telling what is timeless from what is tied to its culture (for example head coverings in 1 Corinthians 11, the holy kiss, foot washing), finding the principle behind a command, and applying one passage faithfully to your congregation.

title.es: La Doctrina del Espíritu Santo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The person and deity of the Spirit. Matthew 28:19, John 14–16, Acts 5:3–4 and Ephesians 4:30: the Spirit as a person and as God, and how you would answer groups in your community that call the Spirit an impersonal force.

The Spirit and the work of Christ. The Spirit in creation and in the prophets, and in Christ's conception, baptism, anointing (Luke 4:18), sacrifice (Hebrews 9:14) and resurrection (Romans 8:11); the Spirit who glorifies Christ (John 16:14); and how this shapes your preaching about the Spirit.

New birth, indwelling and assurance. John 3, Romans 8:9–17 and Ephesians 1:13–14: regeneration, the Spirit dwelling in every believer, the seal and pledge of the Spirit, and the witness of the Spirit, with the Calvinist and Arminian views of regeneration and perseverance stated fairly, applied to a believer who lacks assurance.

The baptism and filling of the Spirit. Acts 1–2, 8, 10 and 19 with 1 Corinthians 12:13 and Ephesians 5:18: the main evangelical views (the Spirit received at conversion with repeated fillings; a second work of grace in the Wesleyan holiness tradition; the Keswick teaching; an empowering for service, as in Torrey; the classical Pentecostal view with tongues as initial evidence; charismatic views), stated fairly, and how your church can keep its unity.

Spiritual gifts and discernment. 1 Corinthians 12–14, Romans 12 and Ephesians 4: cessationist, continuationist and "open but cautious" views, stated fairly; testing the spirits (1 John 4:1–3, 1 Thessalonians 5:19–22); order in worship (1 Corinthians 14:26–40); and a plan to help every member find and use his or her gifts.

The fruit of the Spirit. Galatians 5:16–26 and 2 Corinthians 3:18: walking by the Spirit and growing in Christlikeness, with the main evangelical views of sanctification (Reformed, Wesleyan holiness, Keswick, Pentecostal) compared fairly, and a plan for spiritual formation in your congregation.

title.en: The Gospel of John: Ministry Assignment
title.es: El Evangelio de Juan: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The Word made flesh. John 1:1–18: Christ fully God and fully man, the Word through whom all things were made, and how you would answer groups in your community that deny that Christ is God (for example over the translation of John 1:1).

Signs that lead to faith. One of the signs (for example 2:1–11, 5:1–18, 6:1–15, 9:1–41 or 11:1–44) with the teaching that follows it, read in the light of John 20:30–31, and how you would preach it so that hearers believe.
The "I AM" sayings. The seven "I am" sayings and the absolute "I AM" of 8:58 read beside Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah 43:10–13: what they reveal about Jesus, and a sermon or teaching series built on them.

New birth, believing and God's drawing. John 3, 6 and 10: the new birth, believing, the Father's drawing (6:37–44) and the safety of Christ's sheep (10:27–29), with the Calvinist and Arminian readings stated fairly, and how you would call people to faith in your setting.

The Upper Room and the Spirit. John 13–16: the washing of feet, the new commandment, the vine and the branches, and the promised Helper: what was given to the apostles alone and what belongs to every believer, and how to form a loving, fruitful congregation.

That they may be one. John 17 and 20–21: Christ's prayer for His people, the cross as His glory, the risen Lord's commission and the restoring of Peter, applied to unity in truth and to restoring those who have fallen in your church.

title.es: Josué: Curso Intensivo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Be strong and courageous. Joshua 1: the passing of leadership from Moses to Joshua, God's presence, and meditation on the law (1:8) read in context rather than as a promise of wealth, with a plan to prepare the next leaders in your church.

Rahab, the Jordan and Jericho. Joshua 2–6: Rahab's faith (Hebrews 11:31, James 2:25), the memorial stones, the Commander of the LORD's army (5:13–15) with the views on who He is stated fairly, and how to preach Jericho without allegorizing it.

The conquest and the question of violence. Joshua 6–11 with Deuteronomy 7 and 20: the main evangelical ways of understanding the command to destroy the Canaanites (God's judgment on long-standing sin, Genesis 15:16; the sweeping language of ancient war reports; a unique moment in the history of redemption), stated fairly; why it gives no warrant for violence in Christ's name; and how you would answer a troubled member or a skeptic.

Holiness, failure and grace. Joshua 7–9: Achan's sin and Israel's defeat at Ai, sin that affects a whole people, the Gibeonites and the failure to seek the LORD's counsel (9:14), and how your church can practice loving discipline and seek God before its decisions.

The inheritance divided. Joshua 13–21: Caleb's wholehearted faith (14:6–15), the cities of refuge (20), every promise kept (21:43–45), the rest that Joshua could not give (Hebrews 4:8–9), and the main views of the land promise and its fulfillment (in Christ and the new creation, and in a future for national Israel), stated fairly.

Choose this day. Joshua 23–24: Joshua's farewell and the covenant at Shechem, "as for me and my house" (24:15), Joshua as a pointer to Jesus, whose name is the same, and how you would call your congregation to renew its commitment to the Lord.

title.es: Apreciación de los Idiomas Bíblicos: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Why the original languages matter. 2 Timothy 3:16–17, Matthew 5:18 and Nehemiah 8:8, with Gaussen and A. T. Robertson: inspiration and the texts God gave; the main evangelical views of inerrancy and of how inspiration relates to the copies and translations we have, stated fairly; and why most pastors need appreciation rather than mastery.

The riches and limits of words. With Trench, Girdlestone and Vincent: how words mean in context, the range of a word's meaning, and the common word-study errors (the root fallacy, reading every meaning into one use, reading later meanings back, as when "dynamite" is read into the Greek word for power); and John 21:15–17, with the main views on whether the change between two Greek verbs for love matters, stated fairly.

The beauty of Hebrew. Psalms 19, 23 and 42, Proverbs 10 and Isaiah 40, with Lowth: parallelism, imagery and acrostic poems, how Hebrew poetry is preached, and Hebrew words worth knowing (hesed, shalom, the divine name), using the Genesis 1 Hebrew lab.

The precision of Greek. John 1:1, Romans 12:1–2, Ephesians 2:8–9 and Philippians 2:12–13, with Robertson and Machen: tense and aspect, the article and the connecting words, using the John 1 Greek lab; and why claims such as "the aorist always means once for all" overstate what the grammar says.

Translations and tools. Nehemiah 8:8 and Acts 2:5–11: why versions differ (word-for-word and meaning-for-meaning translation), the Spanish and English Bibles used where you serve (the Reina-Valera revisions and others), lexicons, concordances and interlinears; and the views on the Greek text behind the New Testament (the Received Text and the critical text) and on "only one version" positions, stated fairly.

Using the tools wisely. 2 Timothy 2:15, Luke 24:27 and 45, Psalm 119:18 and James 1:22, with Spurgeon's Commenting and Commentaries: humility, prayer and the Spirit in study, using commentaries, mentioning Hebrew or Greek in the pulpit only when it serves the hearers, and a plan to teach your church to use basic tools.

title.en: The Life of Christ: Ministry Assignment
title.es: La Vida de Cristo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Who Jesus is. John 1:1–18, Philippians 2:5–11 and Colossians 1:15–20: true God and true man in one person, the creeds of Nicaea and Chalcedon, and how you would answer Jehovah's Witness, Oneness and other teaching about Christ present in your region.

Four Gospels, one Lord. Luke 1:1–4, John 20:30–31 and 21:25: why there are four Gospels, the world of first-century Galilee and Judea, and the evangelical views on how to handle differences between the Gospel accounts (harmonization and other approaches), stated fairly.

The kingdom in word and deed. Mark 1:14–15, Matthew 5–7 and 13, and Luke 4:16–21: the parables, the Sermon on the Mount and the miracles as signs of the kingdom; the main views of the kingdom (present, future, "already and not yet") and of whether miraculous gifts continue today (cessationist and continuationist), stated fairly.

Jesus and the Twelve. Mark 3:13–19, Luke 6:12–16 and John 13:1–17, with A. B. Bruce: how Jesus chose, taught, corrected and sent His disciples, and a plan for training leaders in your church on His pattern.

The cross and the empty tomb. Mark 10:45, Isaiah 53, Luke 24 and 1 Corinthians 15:1–20: why Jesus died, the main views of the atonement (penal substitution, Christ the Victor, moral influence, and how they relate), stated fairly, and the evidence for the bodily resurrection and what it means.

Following Jesus. Mark 8:34–38, 1 Peter 2:21–25 and 1 John 2:6: Christ as Savior and example, following Him by grace and the Spirit rather than by effort alone, and the Christ of popular devotion in your region (images, processions, Holy Week) compared respectfully with the Christ of the Gospels.

title.es: Mateo: Curso Intensivo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The promised King. Matthew 1–4: the genealogy, the fulfillment passages ("that it might be fulfilled") and the temptation, showing Jesus as the Son of David and the true Israel, and how you would preach Christ from the promises of Israel's Scriptures.

The Sermon on the Mount. Matthew 5–7: the main ways of reading the Sermon (for example as the ethic of disciples now, as the standard that drives us to grace, or as the rule of the coming kingdom), stated fairly, and one section preached to your congregation.

The kingdom of heaven. The parables of Matthew 13 and the miracles of 8–9: the kingdom already present and not yet complete, the main evangelical views of how the kingdom relates to the church and to the millennium, stated fairly, and what this means for your church's mission.

The church and its discipline. Matthew 16:13–20 and 18:15–20: Peter's confession, the Protestant and Catholic readings of "this rock" stated fairly, binding and loosing, and how your church can restore a member who has sinned.

The Olivet Discourse. Matthew 24–25: the main readings (fulfilled in A.D. 70, still future, or both) stated fairly, and watchfulness, faithful service and care for "the least of these" as the application for your church.
The cross, the empty tomb and the Great Commission. Matthew 26–28: the Passion, the resurrection and 28:18–20, and a plan for making, baptizing and teaching disciples in your church.

title.es: Misiones Mundiales: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: God's heart for the nations. Genesis 12:1–3, Psalm 67, Isaiah 49:6 and Revelation 7:9–10: mission as beginning in the purpose of God rather than in the church's plans, William Carey's case for "using means," and where your church stands in that story.

The Great Commission and the unreached. Matthew 28:18–20, Romans 10:13–15 and 15:20–21: who in the world and in your own region has not yet heard, the main evangelical views on those who never hear the gospel, stated fairly, and why the call to go does not wait on settling every question.

Gospel and culture. Acts 15, Acts 17:16–34 and 1 Corinthians 9:19–23: bringing the gospel into another culture without changing it or mixing it with other beliefs, and the views on how evangelism relates to service and justice (evangelism as the priority, and "integral mission" as taught in Latin America), stated fairly.

Planting churches that stand. Acts 14:21–23, Titus 1:5 and Roland Allen's principles: churches that govern, support and spread themselves, the dangers of dependence on foreign money and control, and the main present-day church-planting approaches compared fairly.

The cost and the call. Luke 9:57–62, 2 Corinthians 11:23–29 and Philippians 3:7–8, with the lives of Paton, Martyn and Livingstone: how a missionary call is recognized by the person and by the church, care for missionaries and their families, and short-term missions weighed fairly.

Prayer, the Spirit and the sending church. Matthew 9:37–38, Acts 1:8 and 13:1–4, with Andrew Murray's The Key to the Missionary Problem: why mission is first a spiritual work, and a plan for your congregation to pray, give and send, as churches across Latin America and the rest of the majority world now do.

The hope of the church. What the New Testament teaches about Christ's return, the resurrection and the new creation; the main evangelical ways of reading Revelation and the millennium, stated fairly; and how this hope shapes worship, holiness and mission in your church.
