title.en: Parables of the Bible: Ministry Assignment
title.es: Las Parábolas de la Biblia: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: How to read a parable. Mark 4:1–34 and Matthew 13:10–17, with Trench: the Hebrew mashal and the Greek parabolē, the kinds of parables, why parables both hide and reveal, and the main approaches (one main point, a point for each main character, and allegorical readings), stated fairly and tested on the ten virgins (Matthew 25:1–13) and the unjust steward (Luke 16:1–13).

The parables of the prophets. 2 Samuel 12:1–14, Isaiah 5:1–7, Ezekiel 17 and Jeremiah 18:1–12, with Matthew Henry and Keil and Delitzsch: Nathan's story, Isaiah's vineyard and its echo in Mark 12:1–12, the prophets' acted parables, and the main evangelical readings of the potter in Jeremiah 18 and Romans 9:19–24, stated fairly.

Kingdom, grace and judgment. Matthew 13, 20:1–16, 22:1–14 and 25:31–46, and Luke 7:36–50, 12:13–21 and 16:19–31, with A. B. Bruce: what Jesus meant by the kingdom of God; the main views of the mustard seed and the leaven, stated fairly; living in a mixed field; grace that offends; wealth and the last accounting; and the hard parables of judgment read without softening or exaggerating them.

How the church has read the parables. With Origen, Augustine, Chrysostom and Calvin: allegory in the early church and the medieval four senses, Protestant preaching after the Reformation, Jülicher's one-point rule and the evangelical answer, the kingdom-centered readings of Dodd and Jeremias, and newer literary, cultural and Majority-World readings, each weighed fairly.

Preaching the parables. Luke 14:15–24, Matthew 13:1–23 and Luke 18:1–8, with Spurgeon and Arnot: sovereign grace and the free offer of the gospel, preaching the sower to a mixed congregation, Spurgeon's own rules for “spiritualizing” a text, and preaching the persistent widow to people in dark seasons.

The parables in your ministry. Luke 10:25–37, 15 and 18:9–14, with Arnot: the good Samaritan, the lost son and the Pharisee and the tax collector preached to your own hearers; stories from your own culture used to open a parable without replacing it; and a sermon or teaching series on the parables for your church.

title.en: Pentecostalism and the Charismatic Movement: Ministry Assignment
title.es: El Pentecostalismo y el Movimiento Carismático: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The person and work of the Spirit. John 14–16, Romans 8 and 1 Corinthians 12:3–13, with Torrey: the Spirit as a person and as God, His work in conversion, holiness and service; and Oneness Pentecostal teaching on God compared with the historic doctrine of the Trinity, stated fairly.

Pentecost and the pattern of Acts. Acts 2, 8:14–17, 10:44–48 and 19:1–7, with Maclaren: what happened at Pentecost, whether Acts gives a pattern for every believer, and the main views of the baptism in the Spirit (received at conversion, or a later experience, with or without tongues as its first evidence), stated fairly.

From Wesley to Azusa Street. With Bartleman: the holiness roots of the movement, the Azusa Street revival of 1906 and its crossing of racial lines, the later divisions, the classical Pentecostal churches, the charismatic renewal in older churches and the newer independent movements, and Pentecostal growth in Latin America and the global South.

Discerning a true work of the Spirit. 1 John 4:1–6, 1 Thessalonians 5:19–22 and 1 Corinthians 14, with Edwards's Distinguishing Marks: why unusual manifestations neither prove nor disprove a work of God; testing prophecy, "God told me" and claims of healing; and the prosperity message and unaccountable leadership, assessed fairly by Scripture and by their fruit.

Do the gifts continue? 1 Corinthians 12–14, Ephesians 2:20 and 4:11–13, and Hebrews 2:3–4, with A. J. Gordon and B. B. Warfield: the cessationist, continuationist and "open but cautious" views, stated fairly, including the readings of "when that which is perfect is come" (1 Corinthians 13:8–12) and the views on apostles and prophets today.

Ministry across the divide. Ephesians 4:1–6, Romans 14 and John 17:20–23: worship, prayer for the sick and order in a congregation where views differ; relations between Pentecostal and other churches where you serve; and a teaching plan on the Holy Spirit for your church that neither despises nor exaggerates the gifts.

title.es: Pentateuco: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Creation and the image of God. Genesis 1–2: the young-earth, old-earth, framework and other evangelical views of the days and age of creation, and of evolution, compared fairly; what all of them affirm (God the Creator, humanity in His image, marriage, work and rest); and how you would teach these chapters to your church.

Fall, flood and promise. Genesis 3–11: the entrance and spread of sin, the first promise of a Redeemer (3:15), the views of the flood as worldwide or regional, stated fairly, and how you would preach grace from Genesis 3.

The God of the fathers. Genesis 12–50: the covenant with Abraham (12:1–3, 15, 17), faith counted as righteousness (15:6, Romans 4), and God's providence in Joseph's story (50:20), with one narrative preached without turning it into a mere moral example.

Redemption and covenant. Exodus: the Passover and the exodus as the pattern of redemption fulfilled in Christ (1 Corinthians 5:7), the covenant at Sinai and the Ten Commandments, and the main evangelical views of how the law applies to Christians (covenant theology, dispensationalism, new covenant theology), stated fairly.

Holiness and the way to God. Leviticus and Numbers: the sacrifices and the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) read with Hebrews 9–10, clean and unclean, the unbelief in the wilderness (Numbers 13–14, 1 Corinthians 10:1–13), and how to preach Leviticus to a congregation that seldom reads it.

The word from Moab. Deuteronomy: the Shema (6:4–9), covenant love and loyalty, blessings and curses, the prophet like Moses (18:15–19), and passing faith to the next generation; with Mosaic authorship and the main critical theories of how the Pentateuch was composed, stated fairly.

title.es: Ministerios Pastorales: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The shepherd's call and character. 1 Timothy 3, Titus 1 and 1 Peter 5: the qualifications, how a call is recognized by the person and by the church, and what they mean for your own ministry or for training leaders. Where churches differ on who may serve as pastor or elder, state the main views fairly.
Feeding, leading and guarding the flock. Ezekiel 34, John 10 and Acts 20:17–35, and a plan for the care of the congregation you serve.
Knowing your people. Visiting and caring for the sick, the grieving, new members and those drifting away (Colossians 1:28, James 5:14–16), and a plan for personal ministry in your church.

Leaders serving together. The New Testament pattern of elders, overseers and deacons; the main forms of church government (congregational, presbyterian, episcopal) compared fairly; and how the leaders of your church can serve together.
Guarding the pastor's own soul. Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 4:16: prayer, study, family, temptation and weariness, and a plan of accountability for your own life and ministry.
Faithful through conflict and hardship. Matthew 18:15–20, 2 Timothy 4:1–8 and 1 Peter 5:1–4: restoring those who fall, leading a church through conflict, and enduring to the end.

title.es: Salmos: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Reading a psalm by its kind. The five books of the Psalter, the titles, Hebrew parallelism, and the main kinds of psalm (praise, lament, thanksgiving, royal and wisdom psalms), with one psalm you seldom preach worked through from observation to application.

Songs of trust. Psalms 23, 46, 91 and 121: what these psalms promise and what they do not, how Psalm 91 is misused (Matthew 4:6), and how you would preach trust in God to people who are suffering without promising that believers will never suffer.

Lament and repentance. Psalms 13, 42–43, 51, 88 and 130: lament as an act of faith, confession and forgiveness in Psalm 51, and pastoral care for the grieving, the depressed and the guilty in your church.

The psalms that call down judgment. Psalms 35, 69, 109 and 137: the main Christian ways of understanding these prayers, stated fairly, and how a disciple of Jesus can pray them in the light of Matthew 5:44 and Romans 12:19.

Songs of the Messiah. Psalms 2, 16, 22 and 110 as the New Testament reads them (Acts 2, Acts 13, Hebrews 1): direct prophecy and the reading of the king's psalms as pointing beyond David, stated fairly, and how you would preach Christ from the Psalms.

The Psalms in your church's worship. Psalms 95–100 and 145–150 with Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16: singing, praying and reading the Psalms; the views on singing only psalms or also hymns and new songs, and on instruments, stated fairly; and a plan to bring the Psalms back into your congregation's worship.

title.es: Teología Práctica: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Grace and the devout life. Romans 12:1–2, Titus 2:11–14 and Philippians 2:12–13, with William Law and Kenneth Collins: devotion as the whole of life lived for God, and the difference between discipline empowered by grace and the "detour of moralism."

Inward religion. Matthew 6:1–18, Psalm 139:23–24 and Galatians 6:14, with The Imitation of Christ: humility, self-denial and communion with Christ; reading a medieval Catholic classic with discernment, and how Protestant traditions have received it, stated fairly.

Learning to pray. Luke 11:1–13, John 14:13–14 and Romans 8:26–27, with Andrew Murray: praying in Jesus' name, in faith and with perseverance; the main views on the "prayer of faith" and healing (James 5:14–16), stated fairly; and a plan for private and family prayer.

The fight for holiness. Romans 6 and 8:1–17, Galatians 5:16–25 and Colossians 3:1–17: putting sin to death and putting on Christ by grace rather than willpower alone, and the main evangelical views of sanctification (Reformed, Wesleyan holiness, Keswick, Pentecostal) compared fairly.

Running with endurance. Hebrews 12:1–13, 2 Corinthians 4:16–18 and Galatians 6:9: dryness, hardship and temptation on the long road; the Calvinist and Arminian views of perseverance and assurance, stated fairly; and the means of grace that keep believers going.

Spiritual disciplines in the local church. Acts 2:42, Hebrews 10:24–25 and 1 Timothy 4:7–8: Scripture, prayer, fasting, the Lord's Supper and fellowship; the views on practices such as contemplative prayer and silent retreats, stated fairly; and a plan to help the believers in your church grow, including those who do not read easily.

title.es: Cristianismo Radical: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The cost of following Christ. Luke 9:23–26 and 14:25–33, and Matthew 16:24–26, with Charles Sheldon's In His Steps: discipleship rather than nominal faith, what denying oneself and taking up the cross mean where you live, and the debate over whether one may receive Christ as Savior before following Him as Lord ("lordship salvation" and its critics), stated fairly.

A devout and holy life. 1 Peter 1:13–16, Hebrews 12:14 and Romans 12:1–2, with William Law and the writers in Holiness Through the Ages (Whitefield, Edwards, Ryle): holiness in ordinary life, and the main evangelical views of sanctification (Reformed, Wesleyan holiness and entire sanctification, Keswick, Pentecostal) compared fairly.
The grace of humility. Philippians 2:1–11, James 4:6–10 and 1 Peter 5:5–7, with Andrew Murray: humility as the root of every grace, the subtle forms of pride in ministry, and how humility grows.

Power through prayer. Luke 18:1–8, Acts 4:23–31 and Ephesians 6:18–20, with E. M. Bounds and Torrey on Moody: prayer as the source of ministry rather than an addition to it, and the views on fasting and on a baptism or filling of the Spirit for service, stated fairly.

The greatest of these. 1 Corinthians 13, John 13:34–35 and 1 John 4:7–21, with Henry Drummond: love as the fulfilling of the law and the mark of a disciple, love for enemies and for the poor, and love in a divided church.

Radical, not harsh. Matthew 23:23–28, Romans 14 and Colossians 2:20–23, with George Müller on stewardship: the difference between wholehearted devotion and legalism, the views on separation from the world, dress and entertainment held in holiness traditions, stated fairly, and a plan for discipleship in your church.

title.es: Rut y Ester: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Loyal love in a dark time. Ruth 1–2 and Judges 21:25: famine, loss and Naomi's bitterness, Ruth's loyal love (hesed), the welcome of a Moabite into God's people, and preaching to people who feel empty-handed.

The kinsman-redeemer. Ruth 3–4, Leviticus 25:25–55 and Deuteronomy 25:5–10: the law of redemption and levirate marriage, Boaz as a picture of Christ and the views on how far a preacher should read Christ into the details (typology and its limits), stated fairly, and the line to David in Ruth 4:17–22 and Matthew 1:5.

Hidden providence. Esther 1–2 and 6, Genesis 50:20 and Romans 8:28: a book in which God's name does not appear, the views on why, stated fairly, the Greek additions to Esther found in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, and God's rule over chance and human choices.

For such a time as this. Esther 3–5: Mordecai's refusal to bow, Esther's risk, fasting and courage, a believer's place in public life, and the debate over Esther's choices (hiding her identity, marriage to a pagan king), with the main readings stated fairly.

The great reversal. Esther 6–10 and Luke 1:51–53: pride brought down and the humble lifted up, the hard questions raised by the violence of Esther 9 and how interpreters have answered them, stated fairly, and Purim as deliverance remembered with joy.

Preaching Ruth and Esther today. Both books, with Watson and Adeney: how Old Testament narrative teaches, avoiding both moralism and allegory, the views on women's roles in ministry sometimes drawn from these books (complementarian, egalitarian and shared-ministry views), stated fairly, and a sermon series for your church.

title.es: Apocalipsis: Curso Intensivo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The unveiling of Jesus Christ. Revelation 1: what kind of book Revelation is, how its symbols and numbers draw on earlier Scripture, the vision of the glorified Christ among the lampstands, and how you would preach Christ from this chapter.

Four ways of reading Revelation. The preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist approaches, and readings that combine them, stated fairly and tested on one passage (for example Revelation 13); what each sees clearly; and how to hold the details humbly while holding the center firmly.

The seven churches. Revelation 2–3: one of the letters read in its first-century city, the view that the letters also picture successive ages of church history and the view that they speak to all churches at all times, stated fairly, and the letter applied to your own congregation.
The throne and the Lamb. Revelation 4–5: the worship of heaven, the slain Lamb who conquers, and the songs of Revelation, and how they can shape the worship and the confidence of your church.

Judgment, the beast and the persevering saints. Revelation 6–19: the seals, trumpets and bowls, the beast and Babylon, the main views of the tribulation and the rapture (pretribulation, midtribulation, prewrath, posttribulation, and views with no separate rapture), stated fairly, and the call to endurance and faithfulness (13:10, 14:12) without date-setting or speculation.

The millennium and all things new. Revelation 20–22: historic premillennial, dispensational premillennial, amillennial and postmillennial views, stated fairly; what all of them affirm (Christ's return, the resurrection, the judgment, the new creation); and how you would preach 21:1–5 to the grieving and the suffering.

title.es: Romanos: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: The gospel and the righteousness of God. Romans 1:16–17 and 3:21–26: what "the righteousness of God" means; the main readings, including the recent debate over the "New Perspective on Paul," stated fairly; and how you would preach the gospel clearly from these verses.

All have sinned. Romans 1:18–3:20: Gentile and Jew alike under sin, the witness of creation and conscience, and the question of those who have never heard (2:12–16, 10:14–15), with the main evangelical views stated fairly and applied to your church's witness.

Justified by faith. Romans 4–5, with Abraham and David as examples: righteousness counted by faith, peace with God and the hope of glory, and how you would counsel a believer who doubts that God has accepted him or her.

Free from sin, alive to God. Romans 6–8: union with Christ, the struggle of Romans 7 (whether Paul describes the believer or the person under the law, stated fairly), the main evangelical views of sanctification (Reformed, Wesleyan holiness, Keswick) compared fairly, and life in the Spirit in your congregation.

Election, Israel and the mercy of God. Romans 9–11: the Calvinist and Arminian readings compared fairly, what both affirm in common, the main views on the future of Israel stated fairly, and how to preach both God's sovereignty and the urgent call to believe (10:9–17).

Living sacrifices. Romans 12–15: the renewed mind, gifts in the body, the believer and the state (13:1–7), and the strong and the weak (14:1–15:7) applied to a disputed matter in your church, with Paul's mission vision (15:14–33) for your congregation.

title.es: Teología Sistemática: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Knowing the triune God. The Trinity from Scripture (for example Matthew 28:19, John 1:1–18, 2 Corinthians 13:14), the errors the early church rejected, and how to teach the doctrine plainly in your church's worship, prayer and teaching.

Christ and His cross. Christ fully God and fully man, and the main biblical pictures of what His death accomplished (sacrifice, substitution, redemption, reconciliation, victory), applied to how the cross is preached where you serve.

Grace, election and the human will. The Calvinist and Arminian readings of key passages (for example John 6, Romans 8–9, Ephesians 1, 1 Timothy 2:4) compared fairly, what both affirm in common, and how to preach the gospel in a congregation where both views are held.
Assurance and perseverance. Eternal security and the main alternative views weighed from Scripture (John 10, Hebrews 6, 1 John), and how you would counsel a believer who doubts his or her salvation.

The Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts. The Spirit's work in new birth, holiness and the life of the church; the main views on the gifts today stated fairly; and how a church can honor the Spirit and keep its unity.

The last things and Christian hope. Death, Christ's return, resurrection, judgment and the life to come; the main millennial views compared fairly; and how this teaching bears on funerals, suffering and mission in your church.

title.es: Adoración Cristiana: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: What worship is. John 4:19–24, Isaiah 6:1–8 and Romans 12:1: worship as the response of the whole person to the worth of God, and the main views on what may be done in gathered worship (the "regulative principle," which allows only what Scripture commands, and the "normative principle," which allows what Scripture does not forbid), stated fairly.

From temple to Christ. Leviticus 16, Hebrews 9–10 and 12:18–29: the tabernacle, priesthood and sacrifices fulfilled in Christ, and what that means for how your church speaks of buildings, "altars," offerings and those who lead worship.

Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. Colossians 3:16 and Ephesians 5:19: singing as teaching, hymns and new songs, the views on singing only psalms and on instruments, stated fairly, choosing songs for their truth, and music from your own region and culture in worship.

Word, prayer and the ordinances. Acts 2:42, 1 Timothy 4:13, Matthew 28:19 and 1 Corinthians 11:17–34: the reading and preaching of Scripture and public prayer, and the main views of baptism (believers' baptism and infant baptism) and of the Lord's Supper (memorial, spiritual presence, real presence) and how often to observe it, stated fairly.

The Spirit and order in worship. 1 Corinthians 14:26–40 and Ephesians 5:18–20: liturgical, free-church, Pentecostal and charismatic patterns of worship, stated fairly; reverence and joy, emotion and order; and the views on who may lead and preach in the gathering, stated fairly.

Worship in all of life. Romans 12:1–2, Colossians 3:17 and Revelation 4–5: work, justice and daily life offered to God, the worship of heaven, and a service you plan for your church and evaluate afterward.

title.es: Religiones del Mundo: Tarea ministerial

topics.en: Paul at Athens. Acts 14:8–18 and 17:16–34, and Romans 1:18–32: the Areopagus address worked through line by line, Paul's two sermons to pagans, how the church has read Acts 17 across the centuries, which bridges to other religions hold and which break, and Jevons's comparative method read critically.

Judaism and Islam. Genesis 12:1–3 and 22, and Romans 9–11: Abraham as each tradition remembers him; the main evangelical views of Israel's place in God's plan, stated fairly; the church's history of contempt and violence toward Jews, faced honestly; what Islam teaches about Jesus, the cross and the word of God, described as Muslims would recognize it; and loving Jewish and Muslim neighbors well.

Hinduism and Buddhism. John 9:1–3, Hebrews 9:27 and 1 Corinthians 15, with Jevons: how Hindu and Buddhist thought developed and the many schools within each; karma and reincarnation beside the cross and the resurrection; teachings that resemble grace, weighed fairly; and witness among Hindu and Buddhist neighbors and in a wellness culture that borrows their practices.

Honoring the dead. Exodus 20:12, Deuteronomy 18:10–12, 1 Samuel 28 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18: Confucian ritual and reverence, the Chinese Rites controversy, the Day of the Dead and Cuban spiritism as people actually practice them, what Scripture teaches about the dead, and Christian ways to honor those who have died without worshiping or consulting them.

Christ and those who have never heard. John 14:6, Acts 4:12 and 10:34–35, and Romans 2:12–16 and 10:13–17: the main evangelical views of those who never hear the gospel (that conscious faith in Christ is necessary, that some may be saved through Christ without knowing His name, and others) and of infants and those who cannot understand, stated fairly; how the church has answered through history; and how conviction drives mission.

Witness among the religions where you serve. 1 Peter 3:15–16, Colossians 4:5–6 and Acts 17:26–27: describing every religion as its own followers would recognize it, folk religion and the mixing of beliefs in Latin America, friendship, dialogue and proclamation, religious liberty for all, and a plan to equip your church to witness to neighbors of other faiths.
